sections.normalized_html: A paint sprayer applies [MATH: 132c\,\textrm{mL}] of paint in [MATH: 8d] minutes at a constant rate. Which expression represents the number of milliliters applied in [MATH: 3d] minutes at this rate?
sections.readable_text: A paint sprayer applies [MATH: 132c\,\textrm{mL}] of paint in [MATH: 8d] minutes at a constant rate. Which expression represents the number of milliliters applied in [MATH: 3d] minutes at this rate?

sections.normalized_html:
The ratio of volume of paint applied to the number of minutes is given by

[MATH: 132c\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 8d\,\textrm{min}]

We need to know the volume of paint applied in [MATH: 3d] minutes. To determine this, we

  • determine the unit rate (milliliters of paint applied per minute), and then

  • multiply by the number of minutes we're interested in [MATH: (3d).]

Dividing the above ratio by [MATH: 8d,] we have

[MATH: \dfrac{132c}{8d}\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1\,\textrm{min}]

This tells us that [MATH: \dfrac{132c}{8d}] milliliters of paint are applied every minute.

Finally, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 3d,] we have

[MATH: 3d\cdot \dfrac{132c}{8d}\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 3d\cdot 1\,\textrm{min}]

which gives

[MATH: (396cd)/(8d)mL:3dmin; (396cd)/(8d)mL:3dmin; (99c)/(2)mL:3dmin.]

Therefore, in [MATH: 3d] minutes, the sprayer applies [MATH: \dfrac{99c}{2}\,\textrm{mL}] of paint.

sections.normalized_html: A solar panel mounting tray in the shape of a rectangular solid has a fixed height and a fixed length-to-width ratio of [MATH: 27\mathbin{:}18.] If the width is increased by [MATH: 14] units, how should the length be adjusted to keep the same ratio?
sections.readable_text: A solar panel mounting tray in the shape of a rectangular solid has a fixed height and a fixed length-to-width ratio of [MATH: 27\mathbin{:}18.] If the width is increased by [MATH: 14] units, how should the length be adjusted to keep the same ratio?

sections.normalized_html:
The fixed ratio of length to width is

[MATH: 27\mathbin{:}18.] To maintain this ratio when dimensions change, the change in length and width must share the same ratio.

The width is increased by [MATH: 14] units. To determine the resulting change in length, we

  • determine the unit rate (change in length per unit change in width), and then

  • multiply by the change in width we're interested in ([MATH: 14] units).

Dividing the above ratio by [MATH: 18,] we have

[MATH: \dfrac{27}{18} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1] which simplifies as [MATH: \dfrac{3}{2} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1.]

This tells us that a [MATH: \dfrac32] unit change in length results from a [MATH: 1] unit change in width.

Then, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 14,] we have

[MATH: 14\cdot\dfrac{3}{2} \:\mathbin{:}\: 14 \cdot 1]

which gives

[MATH: 21 \:\mathbin{:}\: 14.]

Therefore, when the width increases by [MATH: 14] units, the length must [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\textrm{increase}}] by [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{21}] units.

The circle above has center [MATH: O,] the length of arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is [MATH: 7\pi,] and [MATH: x = 84.] What is the length of arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ADB}?]

sections.normalized_html:
We'll solve this problem by considering the following ratio:

[MATH: \textrm{arc length} \:\mathbin{:}\: \textrm{proportion of a full turn}]

The arc length of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is [MATH: 7\pi,] which represents

[MATH: \dfrac{84^\circ}{360^\circ} = \dfrac{7}{30}]

of a full turn. Therefore, we have the following ratio of arc length to full turn proportion: [MATH: 7\pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{7}{30}.]

Thus, the remaining arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ADB}] corresponds to

[MATH: 1 - \dfrac{7}{30} = \dfrac{23}{30}] of a full turn. Our goal is to manipulate the above ratio to yield the arc length corresponding to this proportion.

Dividing our ratio by [MATH: 7,] we have

[MATH: 7π|:(7)/(30); (7π)/(7)|:(1)/(30); π|:(1)/(30)] This tells us that an arc length of [MATH: \pi] corresponds to one-thirtieth of a full turn.

Finally, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 23,] we have

[MATH: 23 \cdot \pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{23 \cdot 1}{30}.]

which gives

[MATH: 23\pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{23}{30}.]

Therefore, the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ADB}] is [MATH: 23\pi.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Ratio questions appear in many settings, such as rates with variables, geometry, and word problems.

Content:
In this topic, we’ll practice turning real-world and algebraic descriptions into proportions, then solving them.

Item 2 — Example: Determining a Rate Using Equivalent Ratios

Example Prompt:
A paint sprayer applies [MATH: 132c\,\textrm{mL}] of paint in [MATH: 8d] minutes at a constant rate. Which expression represents the number of milliliters applied in [MATH: 3d] minutes at this rate?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The ratio of volume of paint applied to the number of minutes is given by

[MATH: 132c\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 8d\,\textrm{min}]

We need to know the volume of paint applied in [MATH: 3d] minutes. To determine this, we

- determine the unit rate (milliliters of paint applied per minute), and then
- multiply by the number of minutes we're interested in [MATH: (3d).]

Dividing the above ratio by [MATH: 8d,] we have

[MATH: \dfrac{132c}{8d}\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1\,\textrm{min}]

This tells us that [MATH: \dfrac{132c}{8d}] milliliters of paint are applied every minute.

Finally, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 3d,] we have

[MATH: 3d\cdot \dfrac{132c}{8d}\,\textrm{mL} \:\mathbin{:}\: 3d\cdot 1\,\textrm{min}]

which gives

[MATH: (396cd)/(8d)mL:3dmin; (396cd)/(8d)mL:3dmin; (99c)/(2)mL:3dmin.]

Therefore, in [MATH: 3d] minutes, the sprayer applies [MATH: \dfrac{99c}{2}\,\textrm{mL}] of paint.

Item 5 — Example: Maintaining a Ratio of Numbers

Example Prompt:
For the values [MATH: m] and [MATH: p,] the ratio of [MATH: m] to [MATH: p] is [MATH: 13] to [MATH: 17.] If [MATH: m] is multiplied by [MATH: 45,] what is [MATH: p] multiplied by in order to maintain the same ratio?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given that
[MATH: \dfrac{m}{p}=\dfrac{13}{17}.]
When [MATH: m] is multiplied by [MATH: 45,] the corresponding proportion is
[MATH: \dfrac{45\,m}{x\,p}=\dfrac{13}{17},]
where [MATH: x] is the factor by which [MATH: p] must be multiplied to maintain the same ratio.

Now, we solve for [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: (45m)/(xp)|= (13)/(17); (m)/(p) ⋅ (45)/(x)|= (13)/(17); (13)/(17) ⋅ (45)/(x)|= (13)/(17); (45)/(x)|= 1; 45|= x; x|= 45.]

Thus, to maintain the same ratio, [MATH: p] must be multiplied by [MATH: 45.]

Item 8 — Example: Maintaining Fixed Ratios in Polygons and Rectangular Solids

Example Prompt:
A solar panel mounting tray in the shape of a rectangular solid has a fixed height and a fixed length-to-width ratio of [MATH: 27\mathbin{:}18.] If the width is increased by [MATH: 14] units, how should the length be adjusted to keep the same ratio?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The fixed ratio of length to width is

[MATH: 27\mathbin{:}18.]
To maintain this ratio when dimensions change, the change in length and width must share the same ratio.

The width is increased by [MATH: 14] units. To determine the resulting change in length, we

- determine the unit rate (change in length per unit change in width), and then
- multiply by the change in width we're interested in ([MATH: 14] units).

Dividing the above ratio by [MATH: 18,] we have

[MATH: \dfrac{27}{18} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1]
which simplifies as
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{2} \:\mathbin{:}\: 1.]

This tells us that a [MATH: \dfrac32] unit change in length results from a [MATH: 1] unit change in width.

Then, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 14,] we have

[MATH: 14\cdot\dfrac{3}{2} \:\mathbin{:}\: 14 \cdot 1]

which gives

[MATH: 21 \:\mathbin{:}\: 14.]

Therefore, when the width increases by [MATH: 14] units, the length must [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\textrm{increase}}] by [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{21}] units.

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We'll solve this problem by considering the following ratio:

[MATH: \textrm{arc length} \:\mathbin{:}\: \textrm{proportion of a full turn}]

The arc length of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ACB}] is [MATH: 7\pi,] which represents

[MATH: \dfrac{84^\circ}{360^\circ} = \dfrac{7}{30}]

of a full turn. Therefore, we have the following ratio of arc length to full turn proportion:
[MATH: 7\pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{7}{30}.]

Thus, the remaining arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ADB}] corresponds to

[MATH: 1 - \dfrac{7}{30} = \dfrac{23}{30}]
of a full turn. Our goal is to manipulate the above ratio to yield the arc length corresponding to this proportion.

Dividing our ratio by [MATH: 7,] we have

[MATH: 7π|:(7)/(30); (7π)/(7)|:(1)/(30); π|:(1)/(30)]
This tells us that an arc length of [MATH: \pi] corresponds to one-thirtieth of a full turn.

Finally, multiplying this ratio by [MATH: 23,] we have

[MATH: 23 \cdot \pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{23 \cdot 1}{30}.]

which gives

[MATH: 23\pi \:\mathbin{:}\: \dfrac{23}{30}.]

Therefore, the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ADB}] is [MATH: 23\pi.]
